newsitem.title: FRANCE: Emirates to lift capacity on Nice-Rome-Dubai route.
newsitem.headline: Emirates to lift capacity on Nice-Rome-Dubai route.

text.p: Dubai government-owned airline, Emirates, said cargo capacity will be boosted on its three-times weekly Nice-Rome-Dubai passenger service when it replaces Airbus 300 and 310 aircraft with Boeing 777-200As later this summer.

"The 777s will be introduced on the route from August 1 effectively doubling the cargo capacity offered by the Airbus 300s and 310s," Jean-Luc Grillet, Emirates director France for passenger and freight traffic, told Reuters in an interview.
On the Nice-Rome-Dubai route the 777s could probably accomodate 24 to 25 tonnes of freight compared to 12 to 13 tonnes for the Airbuses.

"Around two-thirds of the cargo we currently ship on the route is of Italian origin and in particular, from the Milan region. However, the majority of ex-Nice shipments are in the value-added/high density category and offer better yields."
Perfumes and perfume essences, as well as micro chips, make up a good part of ex-Nice loads, most of which is destined for the Far East, via Dubai.

"Nice has been generating 50 to 60 tonnes per month on this route, a volume largely determined by limited capacity. However, we think there is scope to increase this volume by around 25 percent with the introduction of the 777s," Grillet added.
Emirates was gradually replacing Airbus 310 with A300-600 aircraft type on its three-times weekly, non-stop Paris-Dubai passenger service.
"The A300-600, which will be used on every flight from August 1, is a particularly good aircraft for volumetric shipments but overall, capacity will not differ significantly."
Emirates was also in discussions with Air France on commercial co-operation encompassing both passenger and freight traffic but there is nothing specific to report now, Grillet said.

"Clearly, on the freight side, potential synergies are apparent with Air France having a cargo hub at Dubai while there could also be opportunities for making good the two airlines respective cargo network weaknesses in certain regions of the globe."

Emirates continued to play its role as a "niche carrier" for freight in pursuing a strategy of offering most of its ex-Paris cargo space to destinations via Dubai, rather than Dubai itself, Grillet added.

Around 65 percent of Emirates ex-France cargo capacity is accounted for by non-Dubai destined freight. As recently as 1994, 70 percent of capacity was taken up by goods for the United Arab Emirates market.

Emirates "niche" destinations include Dacca (Bangladesh) Doha (Qatar), Maldive (Indian Ocean), Melbourne (Australia), Moroni (Comoro Islands), Muscat (Oman), Riyadh, (Saudia Arabia), San'a (Yemen) and Teheran (Iran).
"The fact that not many carriers serve these destinations from Paris has meant they attract a good level of rates and as a result we have improved our yields year on year," Grillet stated.
Emirates ex-Paris shipments are largely made up of perishable goods and personal effects.
The strategy had been prompted by an abundance of competition with around a dozen of airlines offering cargo capacity from Paris to Dubai.
